common_name: Mrs. Victor Reiter Fuchsia (White-and-Orange Heat-Tolerant Upright Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; named for the wife of California nurseryman Victor Reiter Jr. and noted for carrying its orange-toned blooms through heat that fades many other orange fuchsias.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, out of hot afternoon sun. Mrs. Victor Reiter bears single flowers with white tube and sepals set against a warm orange corolla, on a stiff, upright-to-trailing plant that can be grown as a bush, standard, or large basket. Among orange-flowered fuchsias it is often singled out for tolerating more heat without dropping buds, though like other hybrida types it still slows noticeably in the hottest, most humid weeks of a Gulf Coast summer. Give it steady afternoon shade and consistent moisture, and expect its best display during the cooler shoulder seasons rather than peak summer.

common_name: Trailblazer Fuchsia (Vivid Pink Double Trailing Basket Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after frost danger has passed in rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix in shade to partial shade; a vigorous double-flowered trailing cultivar long sold for hanging baskets by both American and British specialty fuchsia growers.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or shaded container filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix. Trailblazer carries abundant fully double flowers in a vivid, saturated pink along cascading stems that can trail to two feet or more by the end of a season, making it one of the showier double-flowered basket cultivars for covering a large hanging container quickly. Its vigorous, free-branching habit fills out fast but, like most trailing fuchsias, it wants constant moisture and will wilt quickly in a basket that dries out. It has little cold tolerance, so in the Gulf South site it in a shaded, breezy spot with frequent watering and bring it under cover well before the first fall frost.

common_name: Firecracker Triphylla Fuchsia (Variegated Pink-and-Cream Foliage, Orange-Scarlet Flowers)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed in partial shade to morning sun, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or potting mix; a variegated triphylla-type sibling of 'Gartenmeister Bonstedt' grown as much for its foliage as its hummingbird flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade to morning sun. Firecracker pairs clusters of long, narrow, orange-scarlet tubular flowers with striking foliage: olive-green leaves irregularly margined in cream to white, with plum-pink veins and undersides and a distinct pink flush on new growth, carried on an upright-to-arching, shrubby plant much like its relative Gartenmeister Bonstedt. Its triphylla parentage gives it noticeably better tolerance of heat, humidity, and direct sun than typical hybrid fuchsias, making it one of the more dependable fuchsias for hot Gulf Coast summers, and the tubular flowers draw hummingbirds reliably. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and feed through the growing season; treat as an annual or overwinter cuttings indoors in zones below 9.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed in partial shade to morning sun, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or potting mix; raised by German hybridizer Carl Bonstedt in 1905 from Fuchsia triphylla crossed with F. fulgens and holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade to morning sun. Koralle bears long, slender, salmon-orange tubular flowers in terminal clusters above velvety olive-green leaves, on a neat, strong-stemmed upright bush raised from the same Fuchsia triphylla x F. fulgens cross that produced its better-known sibling Gartenmeister Bonstedt. Its triphylla parentage gives it markedly better heat and sun tolerance than typical hybrid fuchsias, and the abundant tubular flowers are a dependable hummingbird draw from summer into fall. Pinch young plants to build a fuller habit and feed regularly through the growing season; treat as an annual or overwinter cuttings indoors in zones below 9.

common_name: Mantilla Fuchsia (Long Carmine-and-Vermilion Semi-Trailing Triphylla Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix; hybridized by California nurseryman Victor Reiter from Fuchsia triphylla crossed with 'San Francisco' and introduced in 1948 as the first cultivar ever registered with the American Fuchsia Society.

directions: Grow in a large hanging basket or shaded container filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix. Mantilla produces unusually long, slender single flowers with a light-carmine tube and sepals and a broad, spoon-petaled vermilion corolla, held among large dark-green leaves on graceful, semi-trailing growth. Its partial triphylla parentage gives it a liking for warmth and somewhat better sun and heat tolerance than most trailing hybrida cultivars, though it still benefits from afternoon shade through the worst of a Gulf Coast summer. It has little cold tolerance, so bring it under cover well before the first fall frost or treat it as a seasonal annual.

common_name: Beacon Fuchsia (Deep Pink-and-Mauve Hardy Upright Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a Victorian-era hardy fuchsia raised by William Bull of Chelsea in 1871 and later Highly Commended in Royal Horticultural Society hardy fuchsia trials at Wisley.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Beacon bears single flowers with deep pink tube and sepals surrounding a mauvish-pink corolla veined red, produced heavily on a compact, self-branching, upright bush from early summer through fall. One of the older hardy fuchsia cultivars still widely grown, it is valued for reliable, floriferous performance in a border or mixed hardy-fuchsia planting as much as for showy individual blooms. It dies back to the ground in colder winters and resprouts from the roots each spring. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, and a heavy winter mulch over the crown improves its odds of returning at the cooler edge of its hardiness range.

common_name: Beacon Rosa Fuchsia (Soft Old-Pink Sport of Beacon, Hardy Upright Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a sport of 'Beacon' bred by Burgi-Ott in Switzerland in 1972, reported hardy to about 5F (-15C) in open ground in favorable sites.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Beacon Rosa arose as a sport of the Victorian cultivar Beacon and shares its compact, self-branching, upright habit, but its single bell-shaped flowers are a soft, uniform old-pink rather than the sharper pink-and-mauve bicolor of its parent, with the calyx shading slightly darker than the corolla. It flowers heavily from June into fall and, like Beacon, dies back to the ground in cold winters and resprouts reliably from the roots in spring. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, and a heavy winter mulch over the crown helps protect the crown at the colder edge of its range.

common_name: Pink Galore Fuchsia (Double Pale-and-Candy-Pink Trailing Basket Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after frost danger has passed in rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix in shade to partial shade; introduced in the late 1950s and a longtime Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit holder among trailing double fuchsias.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or shaded container filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix. Pink Galore produces large, fully double flowers combining pale pink and deeper candy-pink tones, with plump buds and flaring sepals tipped in spring green, set against glossy dark green leaves on red stems. Its vigorous trailing habit and heavy, continuous bloom from early summer until frost have kept it a standard choice for pink hanging baskets for decades. It has little cold tolerance and, like most trailing fuchsias, dries out quickly as a basket plant, so in the Gulf South site it in a shaded, breezy spot with frequent watering and bring it under cover well before the first fall frost.

common_name: Royal Velvet Fuchsia (Large Double Crimson-and-Purple Upright Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; raised in the United States in the early 1960s and long considered one of the most vigorous large-flowered American exhibition fuchsias.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, out of hot afternoon sun. Royal Velvet carries large, heavy double flowers with a crimson-red tube and sepals over a deep purple corolla splashed with crimson, on a vigorous, upright, rounded, self-branching bush with heart-shaped mid-green leaves strong enough to support the weight of its blooms. It can also be trained into a basket or standard given its free-branching growth. In humid Gulf Coast conditions the large double flowers are prone to heat stress and bud drop in peak summer, so give it steady afternoon shade and consistent moisture, with the best bloom typically arriving during the cooler shoulder seasons.

common_name: Prosperity Fuchsia (Double Crimson-and-Pale-Rose Hardy Upright Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; raised by British breeder Clifford Gadsby in 1970, registered in 1974, and a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit holder among hardy double fuchsias.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Prosperity is unusual among hardy fuchsias for carrying fully double flowers, with long crimson sepals and tube surrounding a pale rose-pink corolla veined deeper red, on a vigorous, upright, deciduous shrub with large dark leaves that blooms from summer into fall. Its double flowers are noticeably heavier and showier than the single or semi-double blooms typical of most hardy cultivars, while it retains the same reliable root-hardiness as other Fuchsia magellanica-type hardy fuchsias. It dies back to the ground in colder winters and resprouts from the roots each spring. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, and a heavy winter mulch over the crown improves its odds of returning at the cooler edge of its hardiness range.
